Yes. Dario Amodei recently restated what he calls the “Big Blob of Compute Hypothesis”: roughly seven ingredients that have to scale or remain well-behaved for AI capability to keep improving. He says this is essentially the same framework he has held since around 2017. 

Dwarkesh Podcast
Raw compute — more GPUs/TPUs, FLOPs, larger clusters.
Quantity of data — more training examples/tokens/experiences.
Quality + distribution of data — not merely more data; it needs to be useful and cover a sufficiently broad range of tasks.
Length of training — train for more optimization steps/tokens/episodes rather than stopping early.
A scalable objective function — the learning signal has to keep working as you throw more compute at it. Next-token prediction is one example; RL objectives with verifiable rewards are another.
Normalization — architectures need mechanisms that keep activations/gradients numerically well behaved as models become enormous.
Conditioning / numerical stability — optimization has to remain well conditioned so that additional compute actually translates into learning rather than instability. 

Dwarkesh Podcast
The last two are somewhat fuzzy even in Amodei's description—he describes #6 and #7 collectively as things involving “normalization or conditioning” that allow the compute to “flow” without numerical problems. 

Dwarkesh Podcast
How this relates to the usual “scaling laws”
The famous 2020 scaling-law paper Amodei coauthored is narrower. It empirically studied approximately:
model size+data+training compute
​	
 ⟶predictable reduction in loss
They found power-law relationships between loss and these quantities across many orders of magnitude.

and most supposed “algorithmic breakthroughs” can be viewed as removing something that prevents those resources from scaling effectively, rather than discovering a fundamentally new source of intelligence.
That's why Transformers fit his worldview so well. In his 2023 explanation, he argued that LSTMs/RNNs had structural bottlenecks that prevented information and compute from flowing effectively over long distances; attention removed much of that bottleneck. 

Dwarkesh Podcast

And the particularly important 2026 update is that he thinks the same phenomenon has now appeared in RL/post-training: performance on math, coding, and other RL tasks keeps improving roughly log-linearly as the amount of RL training increases. So his picture isn't really:

“pretraining scaling ran out → we found a new trick called reasoning.”

It's closer to:

pretraining scaling + RL scaling + eventually other scalable learning objectives

all being manifestations of the same underlying “big blob of compute” idea. 

Dwarkesh Podcast

That distinction is pretty fundamental to understanding why Amodei remains so bullish on continued AI progress.
